Hanley1 6 7 Author affiliations: 8 1 Department of Biology, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM 88003, USA 9 2 Department of Fish, Wildlife and Conservation Ecology, New Mexico State University, Las 10 Cruces, NM 88003, USA 11 3 Department of Internal Medicine, Center for Global Health, University of New Mexico Health 12 Sciences Center, Albuquerque, NM, 87106 USA 13 * Corresponding author; cnsilva@nmsu.edu 14 15 Open research statement: To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the authors pledge to place 16 all data and any novel code into Dryad upon acceptance of the manuscript. 17 Keywords: Sin Nombre virus, hantavirus, deer mouse, wildfire, post-fire management, disease 18 ecology, ENSO 19 20 Abstract 21 Worldwide, physical habitats and biological communities are being reshaped by wildfire. Such 22 changes have obvious potential to alter pathogen ecology, yet few studies, outside of those 23 focused on ectoparasites, have tested the effects of wildfire on pathogen prevalence in wildlife. 24 Even fewer have focused on the impacts of strategies for post-fire remediation on pathogen 25 circulation. Here, we investigated the effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on the prevalence 26 and viral load of Sin Nombre virus (SNV) infection in its reservoir host, the western deer mouse, 27 using a study design of matched burned, unburned, and post-burn reseeded sites in northern New 28 Mexico. In total, we screened 411 individual deer mice for SNV via RT-qPCR and analyzed the 29 effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on relative mouse abundance, individual infection 30 probability, site-level prevalence and viral load. Relative abundance was highest at reseeded 31 sites, and model selection indicated that habitat structure – particularly the gradient from closed 32 canopy to open-herbaceous habitat, was consistently associated with increased relative 33 abundance. Similarly, SNV prevalence was significantly higher in reseeded sites than either 34 burned or unburned sites but did not differ in burned versus unburned sites. Viral load did not 35 differ between burn history types, and zero-inflated gamma hurdle models did not identify any 36 strong predictors of viral load. Serendipitously, we were also able to investigate the impacts of an 37 El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle on patterns of infection in a subsample of sites that 38 were studied during and one year after an ENSO year and found that SNV prevalence increased 39 significantly post-ENSO. Both reseeding and ENSO deliver resource pulses that can support 40 increases in mouse density and thereby enhance SNV transmission. The impacts of post-fire 41 management practices on SNV prevalence in its reservoir host that were revealed in this study 42 should be considered when implementing such strategies and when utilizing treated areas. 43 Introduction 44 Wildfires are increasing in both severity and frequency across the globe, driven by rising 45 temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns (Cunningham et al., 2024; Dennison et al., 2014; 46 Salguero et al., 2020; Westerling et al., 2006). Wildfires can dramatically reshape natural 47 landscapes through reduction of ground litter, loss of canopy cover, and transformation of soil 48 chemistry, among many other effects (Bansal, 2025). Following a wildfire, managers may 49 implement strategies to prevent soil erosion, such as reseeding, replanting, mulching or chemical 50 treatments. These interventions may alleviate some negative effects of wildfire, such as runoff or 51 mudslides, but may exacerbate others, such as alteration of plant communities (Keeley, 2004). 52 These wholesale changes in both burned and remediated landscapes have the potential to alter 53 the transmission of pathogens among wildlife, thereby altering the risk of pathogen spillover to 54 humans. In an increasingly flammable world, it is critical to gain an understanding of the effects 55 of fire on wildlife infection. 56 Albery et al. (2021) have laid out multiple, intersecting mechanisms by which the consequences 57 of wildfire could influence the exposure of wildlife to pathogens. At the nexus of this framework 58 are the impacts of fire on host movement and resource availability. For directly-transmitted 59 pathogens, wildfire may enhance inter-individual contact rates, and therefore transmission, via 60 degradation of habitat complexity, concentration of existing resources, or production of resource 61 pulses that support increases in the host population density. Alternatively, wildfire may reduce 62 contact rates through habitat fragmentation, fire-mediated mortality, or production of resource 63 pulses that disincentivize host foraging movements (Fay et al., 2025; Tonelli et al., 2026). Thus, 64 wildfire may shape infection dynamics through multiple, potentially opposing, mechanisms. 65 Although Albery et al. (2021) did not consider post-fire mitigation, it is clear that some 66 management strategies may also affect host movement and host density. In particular, post-fire 67 reseeding provides a large pulse in resources for granivores that may drive surges in their 68 populations, and the plants that sprout from supplementary seeds may alter vegetation structure 69 and plant community composition. 70 To date, the majority of studies investigating the impact of wildfire on the frequency of wildlife 71 infection have focused on ectoparasites (reviewed in Scasta, 2015) or on proxies of disease risk, 72 such as corticosteroid levels (Hing et al., 2017), immune function, or immune proteomes (Black 73 et al., 2017; Bowen et al., 2015) rather than directly measuring wildfire impacts on pathogen 74 prevalence. Two notable exceptions are work by Ecke et al. (2019) and Furtado et al. (2023). 75 The former showed that wildfire-induced thermal stress may increase host susceptibility to 76 parasitic infection in Tropidurus oreadicus lizards, and the latter demonstrated that reduced 77 habitat complexity correlated with increased Puumala virus (PUUV, Orthohantavirus 78 puumalaense) prevalence in bank voles. 79 In the current study, we investigated the effects of wildfires and post-fire management in 80 northern New Mexico on Sin Nombre virus (SNV, Orthohantavirus sinnombreense) infection of 81 western deer mice (Peromyscus sonoriensis). Western deer mice serve as a major reservoir host 82 of SNV. Increases in SNV prevalence in deer mice are associated with increases in spillover of 83 the virus to humans, in whom it can cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) with a 84 fatality rate of ~35% (Childs et al., 1994; Center for Disease Control, 2024). SNV circulation in 85 deer mice is sensitive to ecological perturbations that alter mouse density, as the virus is 86 transmitted via direct, aggressive contacts, primarily among adult males, that can increase with 87 density (Mills et al., 1997; Pearce-Duvet et al., 2006). In particular, SNV prevalence in deer 88 mouse populations, and subsequent human outbreaks, have been linked to El Niño Southern 89 Oscillation (ENSO) events, which drive increased precipitation throughout the western United 90 States, leading to mast seed production of piñon trees, a food resource pulse that supports 91 increases in deer mouse density (Carver et al., 2015; Parmenter et al., 1993). While ENSO 92 cycles provide a well-established example of how ecological perturbations can alter the SNV 93 system within deer mice, wildfire and post-fire mitigation may act via similar mechanisms. 94 Populations of Peromyscus spp. have generally been shown to increase following both wild and 95 prescribed fires, likely due to release of competition with members of their guild and increased 96 foraging efficiency in the absence of ground litter (reviewed in Jones, 1992; Zwolak et al., 2010). 97 Such increases in host abundance could accelerate SNV transmission and enhance prevalence. 98 Consistent with this paradigm, Mull et al. (2023) reported that more rodents were seropositive 99 for orthohantaviruses in burned prairies in the U.S. compared to clear cut or unmanaged control 100 areas, and Gheler-Costa et al. (2022) found Brazilian Sigmodontinae rodents experienced much 101 faster population growth and were more frequently positive for orthohantaviruses after sugarcane 102 harvest fires than in areas where fire had been suppressed. However, fire effects are unlikely to 103 be universal. Sharp Bowman et al. (2017) found that fires in the Great Basin, USA decreased 104 Peromyscus population sizes, suggesting that severe fires may result in unsuitable habitat and 105 decreased host abundance. Post-fire aerial reseeding may further modify these relationships. By 106 providing an artificial resource pulse, reseeding may act in an analogous fashion to resource 107 pulses associated with ENSO cycles, supporting higher densities of deer mice and elevating SNV 108 prevalence (Figure 1). However, as reseeding also alters habitat composition and vegetation 109 structure, its effects may not be mediated solely by host density. 110 These previous studies of deer mouse and SNV dynamics offer the rationale for the central 111 hypothesis of this study, that changes in habitat structure and resource availability mediated by 112 wildfire and post-fire management will lead to higher SNV prevalence within deer mouse 113 populations via their effects on deer mouse abundance. Our study was conducted in northern 114 New Mexico in the southwest United States, a region that has been ravaged by wildfires during 115 the last decade. We tested several predictions stemming from our central hypothesis, namely: (1) 116 relative abundance of deer mice and prevalence of SNV in deer mice would be higher in sites 117 that had recently burned in a wildfire compared to ecologically-matched, unburned control sites 118 (Figure 1A and 1B), and (2) relative abundance of deer mice and SNV prevalence would be 119 higher in sites that had recently burned in a wildfire and been reseeded post-fire compared to 120 burned sites that had not been reseeded and unburned sites (Figure 1D). Serendipitously, because 121 2023 was an El Niño year, we were also able to test (3) whether prevalence of SNV would 122 increase at a one-year lag following an ENSO event (Figure 1C), as has been demonstrated 123 previously in the desert southwest (Engelthaler et al., 1999; Yates et al., 2002). Additionally, we 124 tested whether two other well recognized patterns in SNV prevalence also held true in our data: 125 (4) SNV prevalence would be higher in adult male than female mice, and higher in adults than 126 juveniles (Douglass et al., 2001; Mills et al., 1997), and (5) SNV prevalence would correlate with 127 degree of wounding (Douglass et al., 2001). Finally, although we had no a priori reason to 128 expect a difference, we nonetheless tested (6) whether SNV viral load in individual mice differed 129 among burn history types. To address our predictions, we live-trapped deer mice over the 130 summers in 2023 and 2024 at areas that had burned with high intensity one or two years 131 previously and were or were not reseeded, as well as at ecologically-matched, unburned control 132 sites. SNV infection of these mice was detected via RT-qPCR of collected lung tissues. 133 134 Figure 1. Predicted effects of wildfire and resource pulses due to reseeding or an ENSO event on 135 vegetation, deer mouse abundance, and SNV prevalence in deer mice. The total number of mice 136 represent the relative abundance of deer mice in a given burn history type; red mice represent 137 SNV positive mice; black mice represent SNV negative mice. A) Independent of ENSO, we 138 predict that unburned sites will remain unchanged in vegetation structure, deer mouse 139 abundance, and SNV prevalence; B) Independent of ENSO, we predict that burned sites will 140 experience substantial vegetation loss, increased mouse abundance and a concomitant increase in 141 SNV prevalence due to wildfire; C) When ENSO occurs, we predict that burned sites will 142 experience a pulse in seed production, which in turn will support even higher levels of deer 143 mouse density than scenario B, and therefore higher SNV prevalence; D) When burned sites are 144 subject to aerial reseeding, we predict that this resource pulse will act similarly to the natural 145 resource pulse triggered by ENSO in scenario C. 146 147 Methods and Materials 148 Ethical Approvals and Permits 149 All procedures on mice were approved by the New Mexico State University Institutional Animal 150 Care and Use Committee (approval number 2404001125) and permission was given by the 151 Jemez and Pecos Las Vegas Ranger districts to trap mice within their respective national forests. 152 Field procedures were conducted following the Animal Care and Use guidelines of the American 153 Society of Mammologists (Sikes and Gannon, 2011). 154 Study Areas 155 This study was conducted in northern New Mexico (NM) (Figure 2A), an area that experiences 156 mild summer temperatures with highs averaging 290C, extreme winter temperatures dipping as 157 low as -340C, and seasonal precipitation occurring during summer monsoons and winter 158 snowstorms (Figure 3). Northern NM has experienced multiple large fires in the last few years, 159 including the two foci of this study, the Cerro Pelado fire and the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon 160 fire. The Cerro Pelado fire, which began in April 2022, seven miles east of the village of Jemez 161 Springs, NM, USA (350 46’ 30” latitude, -1060 35’ 4” longitude), was a mixed severity fire that 162 burned over 45,000 acres (Figure 2B). The Hermit’s Peak fire started as a prescribed burn but 163 was declared a wildfire on April 6, 2022. The Calf Canyon fire started as a pile burn holdover in 164 January and re-emerged in April 2022. The two fires eventually merged into one, becoming the 165 largest and most devastating fire in New Mexico state history. The Hermit’s Peak Calf Canyon 166 complex fire burned over 341,000 acres in the Santa Fe National Forest and surrounding areas 167 near Las Vegas, NM (105°20'19" latitude, 35°48'59" longitude; Figure 2D). 168 To assess the impact of habitat alterations due to fire and post-fire mitigation on relative mouse 169 abundance and SNV prevalence and viral load, mice were live-trapped at 3 sites each in areas 170 affected by the Cerro Pelado or the Hermit’s Peak-Calf Canyon fire, as well as 3 ecologically- 171 matched, unburned control sites for each fire, and 2 sites that had burned and been reseeded, for 172 a total of 14 sites (Figure 2C and 2E). Trapping was initially intended to occur at the Cerro 173 Pelado fire sites in 2023 and the Hermit’s Peak-Calf Canyon fire sites in 2024 (Figure 2F). 174 However, in 2023, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) declared the 175 arrival of an El Niño event during our sampling session (NOAA, 2023). To test the impact of El 176 Niño on SNV prevalence in deer mice, the burned sites in the Cerro Pelado fire were resampled 177 in 2024 (Figure 2F); time restrictions prevented the resampling of the unburned sites. 178 Additionally, trapping was initially intended to occur at three reseeded sites, but extreme rainfall 179 washed out the road to our final reseeded site, making it inaccessible. Instead, we re-sampled the 180 site with the lowest trap success (unburned Site ‘U3’) to attempt to standardize representation 181 across all burn history types. The data from the resampled site was not treated as an independent 182 site, but as a continuation of the previous trapping iteration. 183 184 Figure 2. A) The state of New Mexico in the United States of America with locations of Cerro 185 Pelado fire (left black box) and Hermit’s Peak Calf Canyon (right black box); B) Cerro Pelado 186 fire perimeter; sampling area denoted by red box; C) Locations of burned and unburned sites. 187 Burned sites represented by fire icons, unburned sites denoted by tree icons; D) Hermit’s Peak 188 Calf Canyon fire perimeter; sampling area denoted by red box; E) Locations of burned, 189 unburned, and reseeded sites. Burned sites represented by fire icons, unburned sites represented 190 by tree icons, reseeded sites represented by grass icons; F) Sampling timeline; “CP” stands for 191 Cerro Pelado; “HPCC” stands for Hermit’s Peak Calf Canyon. Map was created with ArcGIS 192 Pro. Icons are from Canva free edition. 193 194 Sampling Sites 195 Burned sites were constrained to areas categorized as high severity soil burn, determined by a 196 post-fire BAER (burned action emergency response) survey conducted by the U.S. Forest 197 Service (NM Fire Info 2022). To select burned sites, first 100 random points were generated 198 within high severity burned areas that were within 500 meters of a road and spaced at least 250 199 meters apart. A buffer of 100 meters was created around the 100 points, and sites for which 200 buffered areas were not completely within a high severity burn were excluded. To select 201 unburned sites, 100 unburned points were randomly generated in areas that mirrored burned sites 202 in terms of elevation and dominant vegetation, after which site selection followed the same 203 protocol as for burned sites, save that unburned sites were also excluded if they experienced any 204 burning after 1980, or if they had any visible burn scars upon visual inspection. Both burned and 205 unburned sites that fit all criteria were assigned a number, and final sites were selected with a 206 random number generator, with each burn type replicated three times, and separate control sites 207 selected…

analysis.background: Wildfire reshapes habitats and may alter pathogen ecology, yet few studies examine its effect on wildlife pathogen prevalence.
analysis.methods: The study matched burned, unburned, and post‑burn reseeded sites in northern New Mexico, screened 411 western deer mice for Sin Nombre virus (SNV) via RT‑qPCR, and analyzed relative abundance, infection probability, site‑level prevalence, and viral load.
analysis.results: Relative mouse abundance was highest at reseeded sites; SNV prevalence was significantly higher in reseeded sites than in burned or unburned sites, with no difference between burned and unburned sites; viral load did not differ by burn history; SNV prevalence increased significantly after an El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) year.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Wildfire reshapes habitats and may alter pathogen ecology, yet few studies examine its effect on wildlife pathogen prevalence. Methods: The study matched burned, unburned, and post‑burn reseeded sites in northern New Mexico, screened 411 western deer mice for Sin Nombre virus (SNV) via RT‑qPCR, and analyzed relative abundance, infection probability, site‑level prevalence, and viral load. Results: Relative mouse abundance was highest at reseeded sites; SNV prevalence was significantly higher in reseeded sites than in burned or unburned sites, with no difference between burned and unburned sites; viral load did not differ by burn history; SNV prevalence increased significantly after an ENSO year. Contribution: The findings suggest that post‑fire reseeding and ENSO‑driven resource pulses can elevate host density and SNV transmission, informing wildfire management and disease surveillance. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence

papers.title_zh: 燃尽鼠类:野火及火后重新播种对其宿主中Sin Nombre病毒流行率的影响

analysis_zh.background: 野火重塑栖息地并可能改变病原体生态,但很少有研究考察其对野生动物病原体流行率的影响。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究在新墨西哥北部匹配了燃烧、未燃烧以及燃后重新播种的地点,对411只西部鹿鼠进行Sin Nombre 病毒(SNV)RT‐qPCR 检测,并分析相对丰度、感染概率、场点水平的流行率以及病毒载量。
analysis_zh.results: 相对鼠类丰度在重新播种地点最高;SNV 流行率在重新播种地点显著高于燃烧或未燃烧地点,燃烧与未燃烧地点之间无差异;病毒载量随燃烧史无显著差异;ENSO(厄尔尼诺-南方涛动)年份后 SNV 流行率显著上升。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果表明,火后重新播种和 ENSO 驱动的资源脉冲可提升宿主密度和 SNV 传播,为野火管理和疾病监测提供参考。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未在提供的证据中报告

papers.title: Temporal trends in critical care burden and outcomes of Andes virus-associated hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: a national Chilean cohort.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Andes virus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe disease found in central and southern parts of Chile and Argentina. Recently a case-outbreak of HCPS was reported on a cruise ship, therefore contemporary data on organ support and outcomes is required. The objective of this study was to assess organ support use and patient outcomes in patients admitted with HCPS. METHODS: We used the Diagnosis-Related Groups (DGR) database to analyse patients admitted in 31 Chilean hospitals between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2024. They were stratified by the maximal respiratory support received: no respiratory support, non-invasive ventilation (NIV), invasive mechanical ventilation (MV) or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Hospital length of stay (LOS) and in-hospital mortality were the main outcomes assessed. In-hospital mortality was further analysed by pre-COVID-19 pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic periods. RESULTS: A total of 215 patients with HCPS were identified, of whom 69.3% were males and 87% were adults. Of 148 patients who required respiratory support, 14.2% received NIV, 36.5% received MV and 49.3% required ECMO. Hospital LOS was 8 [3-15] days and in-hospital mortality was 20.5%. Case fatality rates were 29.6% for patients receiving MV and 32.9% for those receiving ECMO. The pandemic period was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (aOR 2.73 [1.06-7.63]; p = 0.045). CONCLUSION: HCPS caused by Andes virus remains associated with high in-hospital mortality and substantial amounts of respiratory support, particularly MV and ECMO. Moreover, the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with a significant increase in HCPS mortality.

full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Purpose Andes virus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe disease found in central and southern parts of Chile and Argentina. Recently a case-outbreak of HCPS was reported on a cruise ship, therefore contemporary data on organ support and outcomes is required. The objective of this study was to assess organ support use and patient outcomes in patients admitted with HCPS. Methods We used the Diagnosis-Related Groups (DGR) database to analyse patients admitted in 31 Chilean hospitals between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2024. They were stratified by the maximal respiratory support received: no respiratory support, non-invasive ventilation (NIV), invasive mechanical ventilation (MV) or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Hospital length of stay (LOS) and in-hospital mortality were the main outcomes assessed. In-hospital mortality was further analysed by pre-COVID-19 pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic periods. Results A total of 215 patients with HCPS were identified, of whom 69.3% were males and 87% were adults. Of 148 patients who required respiratory support, 14.2% received NIV, 36.5% received MV and 49.3% required ECMO. Hospital LOS was 8 [3–15] days and in-hospital mortality was 20.5%. Case fatality rates were 29.6% for patients receiving MV and 32.9% for those receiving ECMO. The pandemic period was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (aOR 2.73 [1.06–7.63]; p = 0.045). Conclusion HCPS caused by Andes virus remains associated with high in-hospital mortality and substantial amounts of respiratory support, particularly MV and ECMO. Moreover, the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with a significant increase in HCPS mortality. papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒相关的汉坦病毒心肺综合征在危重护理负担和结局方面的时间趋势:智利全国队列研究。

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 引起 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS),是一种在智利中部和南部以及阿根廷的严重疾病 (A1)。最近一次在邮轮上发生的 HCPS 疫情凸显了获取最新器官支持和结局数据的必要性 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究使用诊断相关组 (DGR) 数据库,分析了2019年1月1日至2024年12月31日期间在 31 家智利医院收治的患者 (A4)。根据最高呼吸支持水平将患者分层:无、无创通气 (NIV)、侵入性机械通气 (MV) 或体外膜氧合 (ECMO) (A5)。主要结局指标为住院时间 (LOS) 和院内死亡率 (A6);死亡率进一步在 COVID 前、疫情期间和后疫情期间进行比较 (A7)。
analysis_zh.results: 共识别出 215 例 HCPS 患者(69.3% 为男性,87% 为成人) (A8)。在 148 例需要呼吸支持的患者中,14.2% 接受了无创通气 (NIV),36.5% 接受了侵入性机械通气 (MV),49.3% 接受了体外膜氧合 (ECMO) (A9)。中位住院天数为 8 天 [3‐15],总体院内死亡率为 20.5% (A10)。死亡率为侵入性机械通气组 29.6%,体外膜氧合组 32.9% (A11)。疫情期间与更高死亡率独立相关(调整后 OR 2.73 [1.06‐7.63]) (A12)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本文提供了首个全国性智利队列,描述了安第斯病毒引起的汉坦病毒心肺综合征 (HCPS) 的重症监护负担和结局,显示死亡率高且侵入性机械通气/体外膜氧合使用广泛,并记录了疫情相关的死亡率上升,为临床和公共卫生策略提供依据 (A13, A14)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: DNA and mRNA Vaccines Against Hantaviruses: Antigen Design, Delivery Strategies and Translational Progress
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are members of the Hantaviridae family, which can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). At present, no specific antiviral treatment is available for hantavirus infection, while licensed hantavirus vaccines are restricted to a limited number of countries in Asia. This review summarizes recent advances in hantavirus DNA and messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, focusing on antigen design, delivery systems, immunogenicity, safety and translational development. Peer-reviewed studies published primarily within the past 10 years were evaluated together with available hantavirus vaccine trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, with emphasis on Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Andes virus (ANDV). DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated immunogenicity in preclinical and early clinical studies, with an acceptable safety profile. mRNA vaccines represent a newer approach with promising preclinical evidence of humoral and cellular immune responses. However, they have not yet been evaluated clinically. Studies have also reported the potential for varying degrees of cross-protection between hantavirus species, although protection remains limited by antigenic diversity. Overall, current evidence supports further development of nucleic acid-based hantavirus vaccines, particularly multivalent strategies, with emphasis on standardized evaluation and clinical efficacy.

papers.title: Andes Virus: From Transmission Dynamics to Pandemic Potential.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Andes virus (ANDV) has recently emerged as a significant public health concern following a multi‐country outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship in April 2026, with 13 identified cases and three deaths among passengers and crew. Methods We reviewed available literature from PubMed and Google Scholar databases and searched international health agencies, including the World Health Organisation and national public health authorities, for current outbreak information and up‐to‐date epidemiological data. Results ANDV is a zoonotic orthohantavirus endemic in southern Chile and Argentina, with Oligoryzomys longicaudatus as its principal reservoir. Approximately 300 cases of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome occur annually in the Americas. The virus causes severe disease through endothelial dysfunction and vascular leakage, resulting in rapidly progressive pulmonary edema and shock. Human‐to‐human transmission is characteristic of ANDV and occurs through respiratory and salivary routes during prolonged close contact. Clinical presentation includes nonspecific prodromal symptoms followed by rapid cardiopulmonary deterioration. Diagnosis relies on serological assays and RT‐qPCR. Management is predominantly supportive, emphasising hemodynamic monitoring and early consideration of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in severe cases. Conclusions Despite ANDV's severity and high mortality, its epidemic potential seems to be low. However, the recent outbreak underscores the importance of international surveillance coordination and rapid diagnostic capabilities for emerging zoonotic infections.

papers.title: Hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship: Public health challenges.
papers.abstract: •A rare hantavirus outbreak on MV Hondius in May 2026 caused 8 cases and 3 deaths.•Cruise ship confined spaces and HVAC systems facilitated aerosol transmission.•Jurisdictional disputes delayed critical medical evacuations.•Lack of isolation and diagnostics exposed cruise ship medical vulnerabilities.•Pathogen research and robust maritime emergency protocols are needed.

analysis.background: A rare hantavirus outbreak on the cruise ship MV Hondius in May 2026 resulted in 8 cases and 3 deaths, highlighting the risk of aerosol transmission in confined ship environments.
analysis.methods: Study design, sample collection, diagnostic methods, and detailed location or host information are not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.results: The outbreak produced 8 confirmed infections and 3 fatalities; confined spaces and HVAC systems facilitated aerosol spread, while jurisdictional disputes delayed medical evacuations.
analysis.contribution: The authors argue that pathogen research and robust maritime emergency protocols are needed to address medical vulnerabilities and improve public‑health response on cruise ships.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available; detailed methods, epidemiologic data, and full analysis are not provided.

analysis_zh.background: 2026年5月,邮轮 MV Hondius 上发生罕见的 汉坦病毒 疫情,导致8例感染和3例死亡,凸显了密闭船舶环境中气溶胶传播的风险。
analysis_zh.methods: 提供的证据中未报告研究设计、样本采集、诊断方法以及详细的地点或宿主信息。
analysis_zh.results: 此次疫情共确认8例感染和3例死亡;密闭空间和暖通空调系统促进了气溶胶传播,而管辖权争议导致医疗撤离延迟。
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者认为,需要开展病原体研究并制定完善的海事应急方案,以应对医疗脆弱性并提升邮轮上的公共卫生响应能力。
